questions.question: Which of the following statements accurately describes a difference between the right and left phrenic nerves?

options.A: The left phrenic nerve is shorter than the right
options.B: The right phrenic nerve passes anterior to the aortic arch
options.C: The left phrenic nerve passes through the caval foramen of the diaphragm
options.D: The right phrenic nerve has a more vertical course in the thorax

explanation.text: The right phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) has a more vertical and shorter course through the thorax compared to the left phrenic nerve.

Feature Right Phrenic Nerve Left Phrenic Nerve Length and Course Shorter and more vertical Longer and less vertical Relation to Subclavian Artery Separated from second part by scalenus anterior Passes anterior to first part Relation to Major Vessels Passes lateral to superior vena cava Passes anterior to aortic arch Relation to Heart Passes lateral to right atrium Passes over left atrium and left ventricle Diaphragm Entry Through central tendon (caval foramen or just lateral) Through muscular part, anterior to central tendon Associated Ganglion Right phrenic ganglion, sometimes with accessory ganglion Left phrenic ganglion (less common)

questions.question: Regarding intercostal nerve blocks, which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.A: The intercostal neurovascular bundle is arranged inferior to superior as vein, artery, nerve
options.B: The lateral cutaneous branch of the intercostal nerve arises anterior to the midaxillary line
options.C: The innermost intercostal muscle separates the intercostal nerve from the pleura
options.D: The angle of the rib, approximately 6 to 8 cm from the midline, is used as a landmark for needle insertion

explanation.text: The intercostal neurovascular bundle follows a "VAN" arrangement from superior to inferior: Vein, Artery, Nerve.

Intercostal nerve blocks Anatomical Feature Description Neurovascular Bundle Arrangement Superior to inferior: Vein, Artery, Nerve (VAN) Intercostal Nerve Location Inferior border of the rib, in the costal groove Separated from pleura by Innermost intercostal muscle between nerve and pleura (Option C) Landmark for Needle Insertion Angle of the rib, 6-8 cm from midline (Option D) Lateral Cutaneous Branch Arises anterior to the midaxillary line (Option B) Complications Pneumothorax (rare, 0.07% incidence), temporary intercostal muscle paralysis

questions.question: During a pleural tap procedure, which of the following structures is encountered immediately before reaching the parietal pleura?

explanation.text: The endothoracic fascia is the layer encountered immediately before the parietal pleura during a pleural tap procedure. The endothoracic fascia lines the innermost intercostal muscle from inside and is fused with

the parietal pleura, making it the last layer encountered before reaching the pleural space where fluid can be aspirated The order of structures punctured during a pleural tap, from superficial to deep: Skin Superficial fascia Serratus anterior (1st muscle to get punctured) External intercostal muscle Internal intercostal muscle Innermost intercostal muscle Endothoracic fascia (Fused with parietal pleura) Parietal pleura Pleural fluid (to be aspirated)

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with a history of congestive heart failure presents with increasing dyspnea. Chest X-ray is given below. The physician decides to perform a thoracentesis. Which of the following anatomical landmarks is most important to be identified, to prevent damage to important structures at its level?

explanation.text: The Chest X-ray shows a right sided pleural effusion for which the physician decides to perform thoracocentesis. The inferior border of the rib is the most important anatomical landmark to identify when performing a thoracentesis. This is because the intercostal neurovascular bundle (including the intercostal artery, vein, and nerve) runs along the inferior border of each rib.

By inserting the needle just above the superior border of the rib below the intended intercostal space, the risk of damaging these structures is minimized. Pleural Tap: Indications Used for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes in cases of pleural effusion. The fluid can be analyzed for various factors including culture, cytology, and biochemical analysis.

Empyema thoracis for diagnostic purpose Position: The patient should be in a sitting position, leaning forward over a support. Site The procedure is performed at the 7th or 8th intercostal space, posteriorly, at the tip of the scapula. Needle insertion should target the upper edge/superior border of the rib in order to avoid injury to the neurovascular bundle which runs at the inferior margin of each rib.
Needle A wide-bore needle (Abraham needle) is used under local anesthesia. Complications Infection Dry tap or bloody tap Sudden vagal shock Pain and respiratory distress

questions.question: Which of the following structures does not make up the anterior surface (sternocostal) of the heart?

explanation.text: The left atrium is obscured by the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, and primarily forms part of the posterior surface, not the anterior surface.

Anterior surface of heart (Sternocostal) Posterior View of Heart (Base) The anterior surface consists mainly of the right atrium and right ventricle separated by the anterior atrioventricular groove (coronary sulcus). (Option B) The left auricle and left ventricle also contribute. (Option C & D) The right ventricle is separated from the left ventricle by the anterior interventricular groove.

The left atrium is obscured by the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. The heart creates a cardiac notch on the mediastinal surface and anterior border of the left lung causing superficial cardiac dullness The base of the heart is mainly formed by the left atrium (two-thirds) and right atrium (one-third). Major blood vessels like superior vena cava, ascending aorta, and pulmonary trunk attach to the base.

It is directed backwards and to the right, opposite the apex. The base lies opposite the apex and in front of thoracic vertebrae T5–T8 when lying down, descending to T6–T9 when standing. It is separated from the vertebral column by the oblique pericardial sinus, esophagus, and aorta.

questions.question: A 65-year-old male presents with shortness of breath and chest pain. On examination, he has a prominent sternal angle. A CT scan reveals an enlarged mediastinal lymph node at the level of the tracheal bifurcation. Which of the following anatomical structures is most likely to be found at the same level as the bifurcation of the trachea?

options.B: Junction of the azygos vein and superior vena cava
options.D: Superior border of the aortic arch

explanation.text: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is a palpable, transverse ridge on the sternum located approximately 5 cm below the suprasternal notch. It serves as a critical anatomical landmark for various

significant structures and anatomical events. These include: The second costal cartilage articulates with the sternum at this level on both sides, making it a key reference point for counting ribs. It corresponds to the level of the intervertebral disc between the T4 and T5 vertebrae. A horizontal plane passing through this level divides the superior mediastinum from the inferior mediastinum.

The arch of the aorta both begins and ends at this level. The trachea bifurcates into the right and left principal bronchus at this level. The pulmonary trunk divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries here. The upper border of the heart is located at this level.

The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung and empties into the superior vena cava at this level. (Option B) Left atrium of the heart (Option A) lies posteriorly and is located lower than the sternal angle, around the T6-T7 vertebral level.
**Origin of the thoracic duct (Option C):** is in the abdomen at the cisterna chyli, at the level of the L1-L2 vertebrae, far below the level of the sternal angle.
**Superior border of the aortic arch (Option D):** is located slightly above the level of the sternal angle, but its lower border (or the beginning and end of the arch) aligns with the T4-T5 level.

questions.question: All the following are contents of the posterior mediastinum except:

explanation.text: Pulmonary trunk is the content of middle mediastinum. Mediastinum: The mediastinum is an anatomical region between the two lungs in the thoracic cavity. Boundaries: Extends vertically from the thoracic inlet (superior thoracic aperture) to the diaphragm.

Anterior - Sternum Posterior - Thoracic vertebral column The posterior boundary of the mediastinum is longer than the anterior because of the oblique alignment of the superior thoracic aperture and the posteroinferior curvature of the diaphragm. Laterally - mediastinal pleura, which are reflections of the parietal pleura.
It is divided into superior and inferior mediastinum by the sternal plane which passes horizontally from the manubriosternal joint to T4 to T5 vertebra. Anatomical Divisions: 1.

Superior Mediastinum: Located above the sternal angle (manubriosternal joint) Contains critical structures such as: Trachea and initial part of the bronchi Esophagus Great vessels: aortic arch, brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and subclavian arteries Thymus gland (or its remnants in adults) Various nerves: vagus, phrenic, and cardiac nerves, left RLN Lymph nodes Thoracic duct 2.

Inferior Mediastinum: Located below the sternal angle and is further divided into anterior, middle, and posterior mediastinum. Anterior Mediastinum Middle Mediastinum Posterior Mediastinum Lies between the sternum and the pericardium Contains loose connective tissue, lymph nodes, and remnants of the thymus, sterno -pericardial ligaments.

Provides surgical access to the heart and great vessels The broadest part of the inferior mediastinum Contains the heart enclosed in the pericardial sac Contains the roots of great vessels: ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, and pulmonary veins, tracheal bifurcation and bronchi Includes the phrenic nerves and cardiac plexus Extends from the posterior pericardium to the vertebral column Contains important structures such as: (Option A, B, C) Descending thoracic aorta Esophagus Azygos and hemiazygos veins Thoracic duct Sympathetic trunks and splanchnic nerves Lymph nodes

questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents with exertional chest pain radiating to his left arm. Coronary angiography reveals a significant blockage in the right coronary artery (RCA). Which of the following regions of the heart is most likely at risk of ischemia?

options.A: Anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum
options.B: Lateral wall of the left ventricle
options.C: Posterior one-third of the interventricular septum

explanation.text: The coronary arteries supply blood to specific regions of the heart. The right coronary artery (RCA) typically supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, part of the left ventricle, and the posterior one-third of the interventricular septum in individuals with right-dominant coronary circulation. The posterior descending artery (PDA) branches from the RCA in the right-dominant hearts and supplies the posterior part of the heart.

Coronary artery disease is a major cause of death worldwide. It is characterized by a reduced blood flow to the heart muscle (myocardium), depriving it of necessary oxygen. When a major coronary artery is suddenly blocked by an embolus (a plug or clot), the area of the heart muscle that relies on that artery for blood supply becomes ischemic. This lack of blood flow results in the death of the affected myocardial tissue due to necrosis.
The 3 most common sites of coronary artery occlusion are: 1. Anterior IV (LAD) branch of the LCA (40–50%). 2. RCA (30–40%). 3. Circumflex branch of the LCA (15–20%).

Coronary Artery Lesions Infarct Location Proximal LAD Large anterior wall More Distal LAD LAD (Wraparound) Anteroapical Inferior wall Distal LAD Anteroseptal Early Obtuse, Marginal High lateral wall More Distal Marginal Branch, Circumflex Small lateral wall Circumflex Posterolateral Distal RCA Small inferior wall Proximal RCA Large inferior and posterior wall RCA Right ventricular, usually inferior The anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum and the apex of the heart (Options A and D) are supplied by the left anterior descending (LAD) artery, which is a branch of the left coronary artery (LCA).

These regions would be affected by a blockage in the LAD, not the RCA. The lateral wall of the left ventricle (Option B) is primarily supplied by the left circumflex (LCX) artery, a branch of the left coronary artery (LCA), and not RCA.

questions.question: A 50-year-old male presents with inferior wall MI. Angiography shows occlusion in the artery supplying the SA node. Which of the following arteries is most likely affected?

explanation.text: The right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the SA node in approximately 60-70% of individuals. Occlusion of the RCA can lead to ischemia in the SA node, resulting in arrhythmias and conduction disturbances.

Blood Supply to the Conducting system of the heart: Right Coronary Artery (RCA) supplies SA Node (60%) AV Node (80%) Left Coronary Artery (LCA) supplies SA Node (40%) AV Bundle of His Right bundle and left bundle branches The moderator band was supplied by the interventricular septal branches of the anterior interventricular branch from the left coronary artery.

**Left coronary artery and Circumflex artery (Options B and C):** In the majority of the population, it is the RCA that supplies the SA node and not the LCA. Posterior interventricular artery (Option D): Typically supplies the posterior ventricular walls but not the SA node.

questions.question: A transverse section through the heart at the level of the ventricles reveals several anatomical structures. Which of the following structures is most likely to be observed in this section?

explanation.text: A transverse section at the level of the heart's ventricles cuts through the middle of the ventricles, allowing visualization of internal structures within the ventricles themselves and parts of the surrounding structures.

Structures visible in the transverse section of the ventricles of the heart are: Right and Left Ventricles Papillary muscles (Superoposterior, Inferoseptal) Arteries and Veins - Anterior and Posterior Interventricular, Left and Right marginal Sulcus - Anterior and Inferior interventricular Septomarginal trabecula (moderator band) Interventricular septum, muscular part Tricuspid valve, septal leaflet Papillary muscles (Option B) are located within the ventricles and are crucial for the function of the atrioventricular valves.
They are clearly visible in a transverse section at the level of the ventricles, as they project into the ventricular chambers and anchor the chordae tendineae.
**The left atrial appendage (Option A):** is located in the left atrium, which is situated above the ventricles. It would not be prominently visible in a transverse section through the ventricles.
**The aortic arch (Option C):** is located above the level of the ventricles and would not be observed in a transverse section through the ventricles.
**The superior vena cava (Option D):** is positioned above the heart and drains into the right atrium.

questions.question: A 45-year-old male patient is undergoing coronary angiography for chest pain evaluation. The angiogram reveals a dominant left coronary system, with the left coronary artery supplying the majority of the heart's posterior structures. Based on this finding, which of the following statements about cardiac dominance is most accurate?

options.A: In a left-dominant coronary system, RCA gives off the posterior descending artery (PDA) and the PDA supplies the right atrium.
options.B: In a right-dominant coronary system, the LCA gives off the PDA and the PDA supplies the left atrium.
options.C: In a left-dominant coronary system, the PDA is supplied by the left anterior descending artery, which arises from the left circumflex artery.
options.D: In a right-dominant coronary system, the RCA supplies the PDA, which in turn supplies the majority of the interventricular septum.

explanation.text: Cardiac dominance refers to the variable blood supply pattern to the heart's posterior structures, especially the diaphragmatic surfaces of both ventricles, through the coronary artery that supplies the posterior descending artery (PDA) or posterior interventricular artery.

**Right Dominance (Option B):** Left Dominance (Option A, C) Codominance The posterior interventricular artery (PDA) originates from the right coronary artery (RCA). Occurs in approximately 67% of individuals. The PDA arises from the left circumflex artery (LCX), a branch of the left coronary artery (LCA). Found in about 15% of individuals. Both the RCA and LCX contribute to the formation of the PDA or provide multiple branches serving similar functions. Occurs in approximately 18% of individuals.

questions.question: Match the following coronary arteries with the areas of the heart they predominantly supply: Coronary Arteries Supplied Areas 1) Right conus artery a) Anterior 2/3 of interventricular septum 2) Left anterior descending artery (LAD) b) Infundibulum of right ventricle 3) Left circumflex artery (LCX) c) Posterior interventricular septum 4) Posterior descending artery (PDA) d) Lateral wall of the left ventricle e) Apex of the heart

explanation.text: Artery Supplied Region Right Conus Artery (RCA) Infundibulum of the right ventricle Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum Left Circumflex Artery (LCX) Lateral wall of the left ventricle Posterior Descending Artery (PDA) Posterior interventricular septum Arterial Supply of the Heart: The arterial supply to the heart is primarily provided by two main coronary arteries: the right coronary artery (RCA) and the left coronary artery (LCA).

These arteries originate from the aortic sinus. Artery Right Coronary Artery (RCA) Left Coronary Artery (LCA) Origin Arises from the right aortic sinus. Arises from the left aortic sinus. Course Moves forward between the pulmonary trunk and right auricle, descending in the right atrioventricular groove. Passes forward between the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle, and then splits into two main branches.

Branches Right Conus Artery: Supplies the pulmonary conus (infundibulum) and the upper right ventricle. Anterior Ventricular Branches: 2 or 3 in number - supply the anterior surface of the right ventricle. Right Marginal Artery: Largest of anterior ventricular branches - runs along the right margin of the heart towards the apex.

Posterior Descending Artery (PDA) or the posterior interventricular artery: Travels in the posterior interventricular groove, supplying the inferior wall of both ventricles and the posterior part of the interventricular septum. This artery often arises from the RCA but can also originate from the LCA in some individuals. Atrial Branches: Supply the right atrium and contribute to the SA node in some individuals.

Left Anterior Descending Artery (LAD): Travels down the anterior interventricular groove to the heart’s apex. It supplies both ventricles and the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum. Left Circumflex Artery (LCX): Circles around the left margin of the heart in the atrioventricular groove, giving off: Left Marginal Artery: Supplies the left margin of the left ventricle.

Anterior and Posterior Ventricular Branches: Supply the left ventricle. Atrial Branches: Supply the left atrium. Lateral or diagonal artery - larger ventricular branch - may arise directly from the trunk of the left coronary artery. A small left conus artery supplies the pulmonary conus.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man is undergoing evaluation for palpitations. ECG reveals a supraventricular tachycardia with HR of 190/min. An echocardiogram reveals hypertrophy of the right ventricle and enlargement of the right ventricular outflow tract. Which structure separates the inflow and outflow tracts in the right ventricle?

explanation.text: The supraventricular crest is located within the right ventricle and separates the inflow tract, which carries blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve, from the outflow tract, which directs blood into the pulmonary trunk. It is a thick, muscular “U” shaped structure extending from the interventricular septum to the anterolateral wall of the right ventricle.

The crest provides the main attachment for the anterosuperior leaflet of the tricuspid valve. The septal limb of the crest is connected to the septal limbs of the septomarginal trabeculation (moderator band).
**Crista terminalis (Option A):** Located in the right atrium - separates the smooth and rough parts of the atrium, not the right ventricle's inflow and outflow tracts.

**The moderator band (Option C):** facilitates conduction in the right ventricle and contains the right bundle branch (RBB). Helps prevent overdistension of the right ventricle during systole by acting as a stabilizing structure. It does not separate the inflow and outflow regions.
**Interventricular septum (Option D):** separates the left and right ventricles but does not partition the right ventricle's inflow and outflow tracts.

questions.question: A 36-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset palpitations and lightheadedness. Her ECG shows a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 170 bpm. Vagal maneuvers temporarily relieve her symptoms. Atrioventricular Nodal Reentrant Tachycardia (AVNRT) is suspected. The reentrant circuit in AVNRT is most likely located in which anatomical region?

explanation.text: AVNRT is a common type of regular supraventricular tachycardia. It is characterized by a reentrant circuit involving fast and slow pathways, at the level of the AV node. Koch’s triangle is the anatomical region containing the AV node, which is critical in AVNRT. Pathways Involved: Slow pathway: posterior to the AV node. Fast pathway: anterior nodal extension.

Anatomical Landmark: Triangle of Koch: Used for catheter ablation (CA), bordered by: Coronary sinus ostium (inferiorly). Septal leaflet of tricuspid valve (anteriorly). Tendon of Todaro (posterosuperiorly). Circuit Involvement: Limited to the AV node and surrounding myocardium. May extend beyond the AV node, including parts of the tricuspid and mitral vestibules.

Treatment: Catheter ablation targets the slow (Koch’s Triangle) and fast pathways to interrupt the reentrant circuit. Crista terminalis, His bundle, and Right atrial appendage are not involved in AVNRT. (Options A, B, and D).

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with recurrent episodes of supraventricular tachycardia. The electrophysiologist plans to perform catheter ablation. Which of the following structures is most likely to be found at the apex of Koch's triangle?

explanation.text: The Triangle of Koch is situated on the right atrial aspect of the interatrial septum. Boundaries: Opening of the coronary sinus The Tendon of Todaro - a collagenous subendocardial band - runs from the central fibrous body to the Eustachian ridge - a part of the fibrous skeleton of the heart. Septal tricuspid leaflet Importance: It helps to localize the AV node - present at the apex of Koch’s triangle.

Localising the AV node is important to safely perform radiofrequency catheter ablation within the right atrium in cases of AVNRT. Sinoatrial node (Option A) is located in the upper part of the right atrium, near the opening of the superior vena cava, not in Koch's triangle.

**While the bundle of His (Option C):** is anatomically close to the AV node, it is not typically found at the apex of Koch's triangle. It emerges from the AV node and penetrates the cardiac skeleton.
**Right bundle branch (Option D):** is a continuation of the bundle of His and is found in the interventricular septum, not in Koch's triangle.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man undergoes a coronary angiography after presenting with chest pain. The cardiologist is explaining the venous drainage of the heart as observed in the angiographic images. Which of the following structures is primarily visible on the posterior view of the heart?

explanation.text: Venous drainage of the heart - anterior and posterior view: Anterior View of the Heart Posterior View of the Heart Anterior interventricular sulcus contains LAD and Great cardiac vein Right coronary sulcus contains the right coronary artery and small cardiac vein. Posterior interventricular sulcus contains the posterior descending artery (PDA) and middle cardiac vein. Posterior coronary sulcus contains the coronary sinus.

**Great cardiac vein, Small cardiac vein - drain into the coronary sinus (Options A and B):** Anterior cardiac veins - Directly drain into the right atrium (Option D) Right marginal vein - either joins small cardiac vein or directly drains into the right atrium. Coronary sinus: Main vein of the heart’s drainage system, collecting blood from most of the cardiac veins, and draining into the right atrium. (Option B) Middle cardiac vein -drains into the coronary sinus. Posterior vein of Left ventricle - runs in the diaphragmatic surface of LV and drains into coronary sinus. Oblique vein of the left atrium (Vein of Marshall): Small vein on the posterior surface of the left atrium, draining into the coronary sinus. Left marginal vein - accompanies marginal branch of LCA and drains into Coronary sinus.

questions.question: Which of the following veins does not drain into the coronary sinus but rather drains directly into the right atrium?

explanation.text: Anterior cardiac veins are small veins that run parallel across the surface of the right ventricle and open directly into the right atrium, not into the coronary sinus. Venous Drainage of the Heart Venous blood from the heart is drained into the right atrium through: Coronary sinus Anterior cardiac veins Venae cordis minimae (Thebesian veins) 1) Coronary Sinus The principal vein of the heart, draining most venous blood into the right atrium.

The largest vein of the heart, located in the posterior part of the atrioventricular groove (left posterior coronary sulcus). Develops from the left horn of the sinus venosus and part of the left common cardinal vein.

Tributaries of the Coronary Sinus Great Cardiac Vein: Accompanies the anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries, joining the left end of the coronary sinus. (Option A) Middle Cardiac Vein: Accompanies the posterior interventricular artery, joining the coronary sinus near its termination. (Option B) Small Cardiac Vein: Accompanies the right ventricular artery in the right posterior coronary sulcus, draining into the right end of the coronary sinus. (Option D) Posterior Vein of the Left Ventricle Oblique Vein of the Left Atrium (Vein of Marshall) Right Marginal Vein Left Marginal Vein 2) Anterior Cardiac Veins A series of small veins (3 or 4) that run parallel across the surface of the right ventricle, opening into the right atrium. 3) Venae Cordis Minimae (Thebesian Veins) Extremely small veins located in the walls of all four heart chambers, opening directly into their respective chambers.
Most numerous in the right atrium.

questions.question: In a chest X-ray given below, the inferior border of the heart is primarily contributed by which structure?

explanation.text: The right ventricle forms the majority of the inferior border of the heart in a normal CXR, extending from the inferior vena cava (IVC) to the apex of the heart. Borders of the Heart Right Border: Formed by the right atrium. Extends from the opening of the superior vena cava (SVC) to the inferior vena cava (IVC). Left Border: Formed mainly by the left ventricle. Partly by the left auricle. Extends from the left auricle to the apex of the heart.

Inferior Border: Formed by the right ventricle. Partly by the right atrium and left ventricle(near apex). Extends from the opening of the IVC to the apex of the heart. Upper Border: Formed mainly by the left atrium. Partly by the right atrium. Also by the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.

questions.question: Which sulcus contains major coronary arteries?

explanation.text: Atrioventricular (Coronary) Sulcus separates the atria from the ventricles and contains the major coronary arteries. Grooves of the Heart Interatrial Sulcus (of Waterston): Separates the two atria. (Option A)

Atrioventricular (Coronary) Sulcus: Separates the atria from the ventricles. Contains major coronary arteries. Descends obliquely on the anterior surface, separating the right atrium and its auricle from the right ventricle. Curves around the left border and connects with the inferior part. The left anterior part of the AV groove between the left auricle and left ventricle, houses the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery.

The posterior part of the AV groove lies between the base and the diaphragmatic surface of the heart, containing the coronary sinus. Anterior Interventricular Sulcus: (Option C) Located near the left border of the heart on the sternocostal surface. Extends from the atrioventricular sulcus to the notch at the cardiac apex. Contains the anterior interventricular artery and the great cardiac vein.

Inferior Interventricular Sulcus: (Option D) Closer to the midpoint of the ventricular mass on the diaphragmatic surface. Extends from the atrioventricular sulcus to the notch at the cardiac apex. Contains the posterior interventricular artery and the middle cardiac vein.

questions.question: At the midaxillary line, the inferior border of the right lung typically corresponds to which rib level?

explanation.text: The lower border of each lung lies two ribs higher than the parietal pleural reflection. It crosses the eighth rib in the midaxillary line. Lung markings Anterior border: Right lung Left lung Corresponds to the anterior margin of the pleura up to the level of the 6th costal cartilage.

Corresponds to the anterior margin of the pleura up to the level of the 4th costal cartilage. (Option A) Curves downwards and medially to reach the sixth costal cartilage to form the cardiac notch. Lower border: Lies two ribs higher than the parietal pleural reflection. Same on both the lungs.

**At 6th rib - Midclavicular line (Option B):** At 8th rib - Midaxillary line At 10 rib - Paravertebral line (Option D) The posterior border: Coincides with the posterior margin of the pleural reflection Lower end lies at the level of 10th thoracic spine (2 space higher than plerua)
